name: Rafael Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a flexo press at a label printing plant. Flexo means the press prints with flexible rubber plates, onto big rolls of sticky labels, the ones you see on shampoo bottles and jam jars. I load the plates, mix and match the inks, set the pressure, and then watch the colour all shift because the customer's red has to be exactly their red. When it's right, a roll of five thousand labels comes off and looks perfect, and that's a good feeling.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do you see AI showing up in your life right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All over, honestly, I'm the guy in the plant who's always on his phone, but it's for work. I photograph a print and ask the AI how to correct the colour, and I keep notes on every job in it so I don't forget what worked. At weekends I fix e-bikes in my garage for people in the neighbourhood, and I use it for that too, diagnosing motor faults. My wife Mei says I'd marry the chatbot if I could, but the e-bikes pay for the kids' school shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold. Which is true, half the stuff they promised never worked even for me, and I use it every day. I'd say that in the canteen and probably on a forum or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing much, I keep using it the way I do, I keep my job. I'd be a bit disappointed, I was hoping for something bigger to ride. But steady is fine with two kids and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep printing, keep fixing e-bikes on Saturdays. I'd try to grow the bike side a bit, maybe put an ad up at the school gate. The extra few hundred a month is what keeps us out of the red.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the e-bike work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two to three hundred a month, sometimes more in spring. It's not much, but our savings are basically nothing, so it's the difference between paying the mortgage on time and phoning the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever turn the e-bikes into something bigger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I've already got a spare corner in the garage and a second-hand stand. If people kept bringing bikes in, I'd think about a cheap shopfront, but not without seeing the numbers first.

S0.say: AI is a good tool that got oversold, since half of what was promised never worked even for a daily user like him. He'd say so in the canteen and on a couple of forums.
S0.think: Nothing much changes: he keeps his job and keeps using AI as he does now. He's a bit disappointed not to have something bigger to ride, but steady is fine with two kids and a mortgage.
S0.do: Keeps printing during the week and fixing e-bikes on Saturdays, trying to grow the repair work with an ad at the school gate. Relies on the extra two to three hundred a month to keep the family out of the red.
S0.quote: It's the difference between paying the mortgage on time and phoning the bank.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is a heavy AI user who still calls it oversold, which gives his view some weight. His e-bike repairs are a small but vital second income. He already thinks like a small business owner, carefully checking the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, let's get on with it, but train people properly. Machines that set the colour themselves are going to come either way, so you want to be the one who knows them. I'd say that to the lads and to the manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd come out ahead. I'm already doing half the colour work with an app. If they buy a press that does it automatically, I want to be the one running two of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the new press the day they announce it, and ask the supplier's engineer for every manual and video they've got. I'd do an online course in print workflow software in the evenings, there are cheap ones. I'd also keep the bikes going, because you never put both eggs in one basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I like this kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be running two presses. Doesn't that mean someone else isn't running any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Maybe two jobs become one and the other guy is Kofi, who sits next to me. That bothers me. I'd try to get Kofi on the course with me, but I can't make him want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company only offered the new role to one of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they offered it only to one person, I'd go for it. I'm not going to turn down my family's future to be polite. But I'd tell Kofi straight to his face that I was doing it.

S1.say: Great, let's get on with it, but train people properly. Self-setting presses are coming either way, so it's better to be the one who knows them.
S1.think: He expects to come out ahead because he's already doing half the colour work with an app. He wants to be the one running two of the new presses.
S1.do: Volunteers for the new press the day it's announced, gathers every manual and video from the supplier, and takes a cheap online course in print workflow software. Keeps the e-bike repairs going as a second income.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, because he likes this kind of change.
S1.quote: I'm not going to turn down my family's future to be polite.
S1.fieldNote: Rafael sees steady disruption as an opening and plans to move first. When pressed, he admits his gain may be his colleague Kofi's loss, and he'd be direct about it. He keeps the side income going as insurance despite feeling confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, this is serious, and anyone who tells you it's fine is lying. I'd tell people to start something of their own, anything, because a payslip from a factory won't last two years. I'd say the government should help people get through, but not hold my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the press is gone, no question. Colour matching was the clever bit and AGI does it better. Two years is enough to get something going, but not enough to make it pay properly before the job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only about 2 years of warning, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the e-bike work into a proper business straight away, register it, put up a website, take bookings with an AI assistant so I'm not on the phone all day. We'd cut everything else, no holidays, no new phones, Mei would take more hours at the salon. I'd also look for any job going on the repair side, bikes, scooters, mobility chairs, anything with motors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Not frozen, but my heart would be going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a bike repair business even survive, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. Probably not, actually, if robots can fix bikes too. But somebody has to be running the robot that fixes the bike, at least at first, and I'd rather be that person than someone waiting for a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be hardest to convince at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei, honestly. She's the one who'd have to pick up the slack while I build it. We've had that argument before, about the garage taking over our weekends.

S2.say: This is serious, and anyone who says it's fine is lying. He'd tell people to start something of their own because a factory payslip won't last two years, and wouldn't hold his breath for government help.
S2.think: The press job is certainly gone, because colour matching was the clever part and AGI does it better. Two years is enough to start something but not to make it pay before the job ends.
S2.do: Registers the e-bike repairs as a proper business with a website and an AI booking assistant, and cuts all extra spending while his wife takes more salon hours. Looks for any repair work involving motors as a backup.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with his heart racing, but not frozen.
S2.quote: Somebody has to be running the robot that fixes the bike, at least at first, and I'd rather be that person than someone waiting for a letter.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture Rafael wants to move, but he admits the repair business may not survive either. His plan depends heavily on his wife taking on more, a sore point already. He places little faith in government and puts it in his own hustle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, use it. Learn the tools now, build something on the side, don't wait for your boss to tell you. I'd probably make a little video about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is the sweet spot for me. Long enough to build up the bike business, short enough that I'd actually do it. I'd still lose the press, but by then I hope I wouldn't need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 5 years to see it coming, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd take out a small loan, maybe two thousand, for proper diagnostic tools and a better stand. I'd keep the press job full-time for at least three years and grow the bikes in the evenings. And I'd learn the robot side of repair, so when the machines come I'm the one who knows how to set them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can use. Like before a big job on the press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan, with savings this thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the risky bit, Mei would say it before you did. But two thousand for tools that pay back in six months, I'd take that bet. I've done the sums on my phone a dozen times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Leo and Lily to take from this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to see you can make your own work. Leo's thirteen, he already helps me in the garage. I'd teach him what I know, and let him pick his own path.

S3.say: Five years is a window: learn the tools now, build something on the side and don't wait for the boss. He'd probably make a short video saying so.
S3.think: Five years is his sweet spot, long enough to build the bike business and short enough that he'd actually do it. He'd still lose the press job but hopes not to need it by then.
S3.do: Takes a loan of about two thousand for diagnostic tools and a better stand, keeps the press job full-time for at least three years, and grows the repair business in the evenings. Learns the robot side of repair so he can set the machines up.
S3.feel: Anxious in a useful way, like before a big job on the press.
S3.quote: Two thousand for tools that pay back in six months, I'd take that bet.
S3.fieldNote: Rafael takes on debt despite thin savings, which fits his comfort with risk and his habit of running the numbers. Like his peers he expects the job to go, but he sees five years as just the right pressure. He hopes to pass the habit of making your own work to his son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is lots of time, so stop moaning and start learning. And I'd say the government should make the courses free, because not everyone has a garage and a curious brain. Fair is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is comfortable for me. The kids would be grown, the bike business would be established, and I'd have left the press on my own terms. The worry is that in ten years, everyone has the same idea and the robots fix bikes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 10 years to prepare, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan to leave the press around year five and go full-time on repairs, with savings built up first. I'd take a proper course in electric motors and batteries. I'd invest in the business slowly, a van in year three, a small unit in year six, but only if the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It feels like something I can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots do take over bike repair, by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd change again. That's the thing, I don't think I'd be doing the same thing at fifty-three as at forty-five. I'd keep learning, follow the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the plant would you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, still. And the older guys. For them ten years is just a slower goodbye, unless somebody helps them.

S4.say: Ten years is lots of time, so people should stop moaning and start learning. The government should make courses free, because not everyone has a garage and a curious brain.
S4.think: Ten years is comfortable: the children grown, the bike business established and the press left on his own terms. His worry is that everyone has the same idea and robots fix bikes too.
S4.do: Builds savings, then plans to leave the press around year five for full-time repair work. Takes a course in electric motors and batteries and invests step by step, a van in year three and a small unit in year six if the numbers work.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine; it feels manageable.
S4.quote: For them ten years is just a slower goodbye, unless somebody helps them.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Rafael lays out a staged business plan and accepts he may have to change again. He mixes self-reliance with support for free public courses for others. He keeps thinking about colleagues who won't adapt as easily.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to get the bike business standing before the press went. What would help is a bridge, a few months' pay while you build something, and cheap loans for people starting small.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they do on their weekends. A lot of factory people have a skill nobody sees, fixing cars, sewing, cooking. That's where the next job comes from, if anywhere.

headlineQuote: A lot of factory people have a skill nobody sees, fixing cars, sewing, cooking.
portrait: Rafael Chen is 43, runs a flexo press at a label printing plant and repairs e-bikes in his garage at weekends, living with his wife Mei, a part-time hairdresser, and their two children on almost no savings. He uses AI every day for colour matching, job notes and bike diagnostics, yet calls it oversold. He is calm through the plateau and steady change, keen to be first on any new press even if it costs a colleague. Fast AGI alarms him and he rushes to turn the bike work into a business; with five or ten years he takes on debt, retrains and plans to leave on his own terms. He believes in making your own work, while wanting free courses for those less able to.
biggestWorry: The two-year picture, because the press job would go before his repair business could stand on its own.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge of a few months' pay while people build something new, and cheap loans for small start-ups.
